triage.name: Hay Fever
triage.reason: Allergic rhinitis with classic seasonal sneezing, rhinorrhea and itchy eyes; diagnosis reachable by history and exam, common in primary care.

demographics: Slightly more common in males in childhood and early adulthood
Often begins in childhood or adolescence and can persist or recur throughout adult life
More common in people with a personal or family history of atopic disease

risk_factors.text: Personal or family history of atopic disease (asthma, eczema, allergic rhinitis)
Sensitization to seasonal pollens (trees, grasses, weeds)
Exposure to outdoor pollen during peak seasons

social_history: Outdoor occupation or hobbies during pollen season
Living in an area with high seasonal pollen counts

chief_complaints.text: My nose is runny and I keep sneezing
My eyes are itchy and watery
My nose is stuffy and I can't breathe through it
I have an itchy throat and keep clearing it

hpi.onset: Gradual, often over days to weeks at the start of a pollen season
hpi.duration: Recurs at the same time each year; symptoms last weeks to months while the allergen is present
hpi.progression: Symptoms build during the pollen season and resolve when the season ends; they recur the following year
hpi.location: Nose, eyes, throat, and sometimes ears and palate
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; can interfere with sleep, work, and school
hpi.timing: Seasonal; worse outdoors, on dry windy days, and in the morning
relieving: Staying indoors with windows closed and air conditioning
pertinent_negatives: Purulent or thick yellow-green nasal discharge
Contact with someone with a similar illness

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children may not describe itching; they present with clear rhinorrhea, sneezing, nasal rubbing (allergic salute), and mouth breathing. Symptoms can be mistaken for recurrent colds.
Symptoms may be milder or attributed to aging; nasal dryness and medication effects can complicate the picture. The seasonal pattern may be less obvious.
Nasal congestion can be worsened by pregnancy rhinitis, and some allergy medications are avoided. Symptoms may be more bothersome and management is limited.

general.mild: Comfortable, alert, breathing easily; may rub nose or eyes
general.moderate: Mildly uncomfortable with frequent sneezing and nose rubbing; no distress
general.severe: Visibly uncomfortable, sneezing fits, mouth breathing, watery eyes; not toxic
general.critical: Not applicable; hay fever does not cause a critical general appearance

Mild mucosal thickening of the maxillary sinuses

Normal lungs without infiltrate, hyperinflation, or focal opacity

initial.why: Screens for anemia or another cause of fatigue and may show mild eosinophilia supporting an allergic process

initial.test: Skin prick testing to seasonal aeroallergens
initial.why: Identifies the specific pollen trigger when the history is unclear or immunotherapy is being considered
initial.only_if: the trigger is uncertain or allergy immunotherapy is planned

initial.why: Alternative to skin testing when skin testing is not feasible or antihistamines cannot be stopped
initial.only_if: skin testing is unavailable or contraindicated

supporting.why: Mild eosinophilia supports an allergic cause but is not required for diagnosis
May be elevated in atopic patients; not diagnostic on its own

not_indicated.why: Not needed for uncomplicated seasonal allergic rhinitis
not_indicated.only_if: complications or another sinus diagnosis are suspected

not_indicated.why: Low yield and does not change management of typical hay fever
Not indicated unless lower respiratory symptoms or another pulmonary process is suspected
not_indicated.only_if: cough, wheeze, or hypoxia suggests asthma or pneumonia

not_indicated.why: Inflammatory markers are not useful in uncomplicated allergic rhinitis
Not useful for diagnosing or managing hay fever

decision_points: Diagnosis is clinical; testing is reserved for unclear triggers, treatment failure, or before immunotherapy
Antihistamines must be stopped before skin prick testing
Consider asthma or another cause if wheezing, shortness of breath, or persistent cough is present

differential.name: Viral upper respiratory infection
differential.why_considered: Sneezing, clear rhinorrhea, nasal congestion and cough are the most common symptoms of a cold, especially in children and in the fall and winter.

history: Sick contacts at home, school or work
Sore throat and low-grade fever at the start
Symptoms last about a week and resolve rather than recurring each year at the same time
No prominent itching of the eyes, nose or palate
exam: Erythematous nasal mucosa rather than pale and boggy
Injected posterior pharynx with exudate or enlarged tender cervical nodes
labs: Viral testing only if it would change management

differential.name: Nonallergic (vasomotor) rhinitis
differential.why_considered: Chronic or recurrent clear rhinorrhea and congestion without an obvious seasonal trigger.

history: Symptoms year-round or triggered by temperature changes, odors, alcohol, spicy foods or stress
Little or no itching of the eyes, nose or palate
No clear seasonal pattern and no personal or family history of atopy
exam: Nasal mucosa may be erythematous or normal rather than pale and boggy
labs: Negative skin prick testing and normal allergen-specific IgE

differential.name: Acute bacterial sinusitis
differential.why_considered: Nasal congestion and discharge with facial pressure can be mistaken for severe hay fever, and allergic rhinitis predisposes to sinusitis.

history: Symptoms for more than 10 days without improvement, or worse after initial improvement
Thick yellow-green or purulent nasal discharge
Facial pain or pressure, often unilateral, worse when bending forward
Fever and reduced sense of smell
exam: Tenderness over the frontal or maxillary sinuses
Purulent discharge in the nasal cavity or posterior pharynx
imaging: CT sinuses showing air-fluid levels or mucosal thickening when complications are suspected

differential.name: Allergic conjunctivitis
differential.why_considered: Itchy, watery, red eyes are a hallmark of hay fever and can occur alone or with mild nasal symptoms.

history: Eye symptoms dominate and nasal symptoms are minimal
Bilateral itching and tearing with seasonal or perennial triggers
exam: Cobblestone papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva in chronic cases
No purulent discharge or corneal involvement

differential.name: Bacterial conjunctivitis
differential.why_considered: Red, watery eyes can be caused by infection rather than allergy.

history: Thick purulent discharge that sticks the eyelids together in the morning
Unilateral or asymmetric onset
No itching and no seasonal pattern
exam: Purulent discharge on the lids and lashes
Conjunctival injection without significant tearing or chemosis

differential.name: Nasal foreign body
differential.why_considered: Unilateral nasal obstruction and discharge in a young child can be mistaken for allergy.
differential.trigger: Unilateral nasal obstruction or foul-smelling discharge in a child

history: Unilateral obstruction and discharge
Foul or bloody odor noticed by parents
No seasonal pattern or itching
exam: Visible foreign body or unilateral mucosal inflammation on nasal inspection
imaging: Rarely needed; CT or plain film only if a radiopaque object or complication is suspected

differential.name: Nasal polyps
differential.why_considered: Chronic nasal obstruction and reduced smell can be attributed to allergy.

history: Progressive, persistent nasal obstruction over months
Reduced or absent sense of smell
May be associated with asthma or aspirin sensitivity
exam: Pale, translucent, grape-like masses in the nasal cavity
Little or no itching or sneezing
imaging: CT sinuses showing polypoid mucosal disease and sinus opacification

differential.name: Cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhea
differential.why_considered: Clear watery nasal drainage can be mistaken for allergic rhinorrhea.
differential.trigger: Clear drainage that is unilateral, worse when leaning forward, or follows head trauma or sinus surgery

history: Recent head trauma, sinus or skull base surgery
Drainage worse when bending forward or straining
Headache or history of meningitis
exam: No itching, sneezing or conjunctival symptoms
labs: Nasal fluid positive for beta-2 transferrin
imaging: High-resolution CT or MRI of the skull base showing a defect

severity.mild: Intermittent sneezing, clear rhinorrhea and itchy eyes that are noticed but do not interfere with sleep, school, work or daily activities; exam shows mild nasal mucosal pallor and no complications.
severity.moderate: Daily symptoms that interfere with sleep, concentration or activities; prominent congestion, sneezing and itchy watery eyes; exam shows pale boggy nasal mucosa and conjunctival injection.
severity.severe: Persistent, bothersome symptoms despite first-line antihistamines and nasal steroids, with poor sleep, daytime fatigue, reduced school or work performance, and frequent use of rescue medications; may be accompanied by asthma or recurrent sinusitis.
severity.critical: Not applicable; hay fever itself is not life-threatening. A critical presentation should prompt evaluation for anaphylaxis, severe asthma exacerbation or another diagnosis.

red_flags.finding: Unilateral nasal obstruction, bleeding or foul-smelling discharge
red_flags.meaning: Suggests a foreign body, polyp or tumor rather than simple allergic rhinitis

red_flags.finding: Fever, purulent nasal discharge or facial pain and pressure
red_flags.meaning: Suggests acute bacterial sinusitis or another infection

red_flags.finding: Wheezing, shortness of breath or chest tightness
red_flags.meaning: Suggests asthma or another lower respiratory process rather than isolated hay fever

red_flags.finding: Clear rhinorrhea after head trauma or sinus surgery, or drainage worse when leaning forward
Loss of smell, vision changes or severe headache
red_flags.meaning: Suggests a complication such as sinusitis with orbital or intracranial extension, or another diagnosis

complications.name: Acute or chronic sinusitis
clues: Symptoms lasting more than 10 days or worsening after initial improvement

complications.name: Otitis media with effusion
clues: Fluid behind the tympanic membrane on otoscopy

complications.name: Asthma exacerbation
clues: Shortness of breath during pollen season

special_populations.differences: Young children may not describe itching and present with clear rhinorrhea, sneezing, nasal rubbing (allergic salute) and mouth breathing; symptoms are often mistaken for recurrent colds. Untreated disease can contribute to otitis media with effusion and poor sleep.

Symptoms may be milder or attributed to aging, and the seasonal pattern may be less obvious. Nasal dryness and medication effects (such as antihypertensives) can complicate the picture, and sedating antihistamines should be avoided.

Nasal congestion may be worsened by pregnancy rhinitis, and some allergy medications are avoided. Intranasal corticosteroids and second-generation antihistamines are generally preferred; immunotherapy is usually not started during pregnancy.

key_questions.question: When do your symptoms happen — is there a time of year they always come back?
key_questions.looking_for: A recurring seasonal pattern (spring tree pollen, summer grass pollen, late summer/fall weed pollen) rather than year-round or a one-off illness

key_questions.question: Do your eyes, nose, or throat itch?
key_questions.looking_for: Prominent itching of the eyes, nose, or palate — the hallmark that separates allergy from infection

key_questions.question: What does the nasal discharge look like?
key_questions.looking_for: Clear, watery discharge; thick yellow-green purulent discharge suggests infection

key_questions.question: What makes your symptoms better or worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Worse outdoors, on dry windy days, with mowing or gardening; better indoors with windows closed and air conditioning, or with antihistamines

key_questions.question: How long do the symptoms last each time they start?
key_questions.looking_for: Weeks to months while the pollen is in the air, then resolution; a cold lasts about a week

key_questions.question: Do you have sneezing fits, and how often?
key_questions.looking_for: Frequent paroxysmal sneezing, often in the morning or after going outdoors

key_questions.question: Do you have a cough, wheezing, or shortness of breath?
key_questions.looking_for: Cough from postnasal drip is common; wheezing or shortness of breath suggests asthma and changes management

key_questions.question: Do you have any facial pain or pressure, fever, or loss of smell?
key_questions.looking_for: These suggest bacterial sinusitis or another complication rather than uncomplicated hay fever

key_questions.question: Do you have any blockage or bleeding from just one side of your nose?
key_questions.looking_for: Unilateral obstruction, bleeding, or foul discharge suggests a foreign body, polyp, or tumor

key_questions.question: Do you have asthma, eczema, or other allergies? Does anyone in your family?
key_questions.looking_for: A personal or family history of atopic disease supports the diagnosis

key_questions.question: What have you tried for this, and did it help?
key_questions.looking_for: Response to antihistamines or nasal steroids supports an allergic cause and guides treatment

key_questions.question: Do you spend a lot of time outdoors, or do you have hobbies like gardening or mowing?
key_questions.looking_for: Outdoor exposure during pollen season that fits the seasonal pattern

reasoning_points: Recurrent symptoms that occur at the same time each year, matching a pollen season
Prominent itching of the eyes, nose, or palate, which points away from infection
Clear, watery rhinorrhea with sneezing fits and nasal congestion
Itchy, watery, red eyes (allergic conjunctivitis) accompanying the nasal symptoms
Personal or family history of atopic disease such as asthma or eczema
Exam shows pale, boggy nasal mucosa with clear discharge and no purulent discharge or sinus tenderness
No fever, facial pain, or unilateral findings to suggest infection, foreign body, or another cause
Symptoms improve with antihistamines or nasal corticosteroids and with avoidance of the allergen

easy: Clear seasonal pattern with symptoms every spring or fall
Prominent itchy, watery eyes and sneezing fits
Pale, boggy nasal mucosa with clear discharge on exam
Personal or family history of atopy
medium: Symptoms overlap with a cold or with year-round nonallergic rhinitis
Patient cannot clearly describe a seasonal pattern
Mild cough and postnasal drip raise the question of asthma
Young child who cannot describe itching and presents with clear rhinorrhea and nasal rubbing
hard: Older adult with milder symptoms attributed to aging or medications
Pregnant patient with congestion worsened by pregnancy rhinitis and limited medication options
Symptoms that persist more than 10 days or worsen after improving, suggesting bacterial sinusitis
Unilateral obstruction or clear drainage after head trauma, suggesting a foreign body or CSF leak
